title: Wrath and patience
hook: anger isn't wrong in itself; rage that wants harm is

segments.voice: Yesterday, envy and kindness: Saul eyed David, and Jonathan gave him his robe. Your line was their joy is mine. Who did you congratulate? Day one thousand two hundred three.

A prophet is furious with God. His name is Jonah. He was sent to warn the great city of Nineveh, he finally went, and it worked. The people turned around, and God spared them. And Jonah is livid. Listen to why. He prays, and in the King James words he says: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness." That's his complaint. He's angry that God isn't angry. Then God answers him with one short question: "Doest thou well to be angry?" Today: wrath and patience.

Notice what God doesn't say. He doesn't say, never be angry. He asks whether this anger is doing well. That's the line Christian teaching draws. Anger itself is not the sin. Mark's Gospel says Jesus once looked round on a room "with anger," and in the same verse, that he was grieved. And Paul writes something that sounds almost like permission: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Be angry. And sin not. So where's the line? The old teachers put it here. Anger rises at something wrong: an injustice, a cruelty, a lie. That can be clean. It can be the energy that makes a person stand up for someone. It turns into wrath when it stops wanting the wrong fixed and starts wanting someone hurt. When it rehearses the argument at 2am. When it keeps score. When the sun goes down on it, and comes up on it, and goes down on it again. Paul's sunset is a deadline: don't carry it to bed. The answer the tradition gives is patience, and the Bible has a phrase for it, the very one Jonah threw back at God: slow to anger. A psalm says it about God: "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy." And Proverbs turns it into a kind of strength: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Slow is the key word. Not never. Slow. The anger can still come. It just doesn't get to drive. James puts it in a sequence anyone can try: "swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Hear first. Speak later. Get angry last, if at all.

Here's the practice: count to ten once. Settle, and breathe. Bring back one small thing that made you angry this week. Not the biggest. A driver, a reply, a tone of voice. Let it come up. Now, before you do anything with it, count ten slow breaths. One. Two. All the way. Somewhere around six or seven, ask Jonah's question: is this anger doing well? If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words: slow to anger, plenteous in mercy. The bell holds the time.
Wrath and patience. Anger that wants harm, and the strength to be slow to anger, the way the psalm says God is.
Your line: slow to anger. Today, when the heat rises, hear first, speak later, and don't let the sun go down on it. Day one thousand two hundred three.

howItsDone: Christian teaching on the deadly sins names wrath, anger that seeks harm, and pairs it with patience; some Christians bring a grudge to confession or prayer, and some make a habit of settling a quarrel before the day ends, after Ephesians 4:26.

myth: the Bible treats every kind of anger as a sin
Paul writes "be ye angry, and sin not." anger turns to wrath when it wants harm.
Jonah was angry because God was merciful
he says it himself: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger."
"slow to anger" is said about God in the Psalms
"the LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy."

fork.setup: you're Jonah. the city you warned has been spared, and you're furious about it. God asks, "doest thou well to be angry?" what do you do?
options: go out of the city and sit down to see what will happen to it.
go back in and warn them again.
fork.reveal: Jonah doesn't answer. he walks out, builds a little shelter east of the city, and sits to see what will become of it. the book ends with God still asking him questions.

original.note: Hebrew: slow to anger, the phrase in Jonah 4:2 and Psalm 103:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: good Christians never get angry.
what it means: anger isn't the sin. it turns to wrath when it wants someone hurt. the answer is to be slow to anger.
what a scholar hears: erekh appayim, slow to anger, the phrase used of God that Jonah throws back at him in Jonah 4:2.

notes: Avoids Matthew 5:22, used on day 1189 (do not kill). Confirm no overlap.
'The old teachers put it here' summarizes the classical distinction (e.g. Aquinas, Summa II-II q.158) between anger at wrong and anger that seeks harm; no specific teacher is quoted. Confirm.

Mark 11:15 (tables of the money changers) is paraphrased as Jesus being angry; the text describes the action, not the emotion. Confirm the framing, or swap in Mark 3:5 ('looked round about on them with anger').
Original note gives the lexicon sense of אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם (long of nostrils/face); this is an etymology in the game only, not spoken. Confirm or trim to 'slow to anger'.
Fork reveal: Jonah 4:5 (booth on the east side of the city); 'the book ends with God still asking him questions' refers to 4:10–11 ending in a question. Confirm.

Editor pass: Jesus's anger now rests on Mark 3:5 ('with anger', quoted) instead of the temple tables, where the text names no emotion; the Original note's 'long of nostrils' etymology cut; 'lovely phrase' trimmed; howItsDone 'many Christians' softened to 'some'.

Audit (2026-10-02): hook no longer seats Jonah 'on a hill outside the city' while he prays: in Jonah 4 he prays first (4:2-3) and only goes out to sit east of the city at 4:5, and no hill is named. Myth reworded from 'Christian teaching says every kind of anger is a sin' to 'the Bible treats...', since some Christian teachers (e.g. Cassian, Institutes 8) counseled against all anger; the reveal cites Paul. The earlier Mark 11:15 note is superseded (Mark 3:5 is used).
